title: RETURNING, upsert with ON CONFLICT, MERGE
summary: RETURNING reads back what you wrote in the same statement. ON CONFLICT makes an insert an upsert; MERGE expresses insert/update/delete in one pass with a join condition.

examples.title: Upsert stock levels and read back the affected rows

annotations.note: One statement: insert the new sku, refresh the existing one. The conflict target (sku) must be a unique constraint — a conflict the database never sees can't be upserted.
qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty: existing row plus incoming amount. EXCLUDED is the row that *would have* been inserted.
RETURNING fires once per affected row, after the update or insert — including OLD/NEW in PG 18 for both sides of the change.
MERGE joins source to target and picks an action per row. Use it when the decision is "match by X, then insert/update/delete"; plain ON CONFLICT when it's just insert-or-update.

use_cases: Idempotent ingest: re-running a load must not duplicate rows
Counters and stock: qty = qty + n without read-modify-write races (with FOR UPDATE or in one statement)
API responses that echo the written rows without a second round-trip
strengths: Atomic: no window where a concurrent reader sees the old value between your UPDATE and INSERT
RETURNING eliminates the follow-up SELECT and its race
MERGE covers insert+update+delete in one declarative pass (PG 17 adds MERGE ... RETURNING)
weaknesses: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING hides *why* nothing happened; you still need RETURNING to know
MERGE requires PG 15+; ON CONFLICT remains the portable workhorse
Uperts on hot rows serialize on the row lock — batch bursts can queue

pitfalls.title: ON CONFLICT without a conflict target
pitfalls.detail: DO UPDATE needs (sku) — without it the statement can't know which unique constraint to arbitrate.

pitfalls.title: Assuming RETURNING shows the pre-image
pitfalls.detail: It returns the new row. PG 18's RETURNING OLD/NEW gives both, explicitly.

quiz.q: What does EXCLUDED refer to in ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE?
options: The row that would have been inserted
quiz.why: EXCLUDED carries the proposed insert, so you can combine it with the current row.

quiz.q: RETURNING in an UPDATE gives you…
quiz.why: Default is the post-image; PG 18 adds RETURNING OLD.* / NEW.* for both sides.

body:
## Concept

`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` turns a would-be duplicate into an update (`DO UPDATE`) or a no-op
(`DO NOTHING`); `RETURNING` streams the affected rows back out of the same statement.
`MERGE` (PG 15+) joins a source and picks per-row actions.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- App code: the SELECT-then-INSERT-else-UPDATE dance is a race; ON CONFLICT does it in one
  atomic statement.
- Go/TS: RETURNING replaces the "insert, then query by id" round trip — one statement, one
  network hop, no interleaving window.

## Design notes

Upserts are the idiomatic answer to *idempotency*: replaying an event stream or a CSV load
must converge, not duplicate. But decide conflict behavior deliberately — DO NOTHING can
mask bugs where the same key means different things. When the logic grows beyond
insert-or-update (deletes, conditions across tables), that's MERGE's shape.

expected.upsert-returning:
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
INSERT 0 2
    sku    | qty
    -------+----
    widget | 15
    gizmo  | 7
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
MERGE 2
    merge_action | sku    | qty
    -------------+--------+----
    UPDATE       | gadget | 1
    INSERT       | doodad | 1
